## Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity

Sometimes researchers want to compare the distribution of a categorical variable across two or more populations or groups. A chi-square test for homogeneity is used to determine whether the distribution of a categorical variable is the same for all populations being compared. For example, a college may want to determine whether preferred learning format (in-person, online, or hybrid) differs among students from different class years. Similarly, a company may wish to compare customer satisfaction ratings across several store locations.

Although the data are typically summarized in a two-way table, the goal differs from a test for independence. In a test for independence, we examine whether two categorical variables are associated within a single population. In a test for homogeneity, we compare the distribution of one categorical variable across multiple populations or groups.

As with the chi-square goodness-of-fit test and the chi-square test for independence, the chi-square test for homogeneity compares observed counts to expected counts. Large differences between the observed and expected counts provide evidence that the distributions are not the same across the populations.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Conditions for Test of Homogeneity

The conditions for a chi-square test for homogeneity are nearly identical to those for a chi-square test for independence. The primary difference is the first condition. In a test for homogeneity, the data come from two or more populations or groups being compared, whereas in a test for independence, the data come from a single population and involve two categorical variables measured on each individual. The conditions are listed below.

1.  Categorical data: The response variable is categorical, and the data consist of counts for each category within two or more populations or groups.
2.  Randomness: The data should come from a random sample or a randomized process.
3.  Independence: The observations should be independent. When sampling without replacement from a finite population, the sample should generally be no more than 10% of the population.
4.  Expected counts: The expected counts must be sufficiently large for the chi-square distribution to provide a reasonable approximation. A commonly used guideline is that each expected count should be at least 5.

:::

### Null and Alternative Hypotheses

Before conducting a chi-square test for homogeneity, we must state the null and alternative hypotheses. These hypotheses address whether the distribution of the categorical variable is the same across the populations or groups being compared.

The null hypothesis states that the population distributions are identical across all groups. In other words, the proportions in each category are the same for every population. The alternative hypothesis states that the distributions are not all the same, meaning that at least one population has different category proportions.

Because the hypotheses compare distributions across populations, they are typically stated in words rather than mathematical notation.

$$ \begin{aligned}
H_0 &: \text{The distribution of the categorical variable is the same for all populations (or groups).} \\
H_a &: \text{The distribution of the categorical variable is not the same for all populations (or groups).}
\end{aligned} $$

::: callout-note
## Hypotheses for Test of Homogeneity

The hypotheses should be written in the context of the problem. Be specific about the populations and the categorical variable being compared.

:::

::: {#exm-customer-satisfaction}
## Customer Satisfaction

A company operates three retail store locations and wants to compare customer satisfaction among the stores. A random sample of customers is selected from each location and asked to rate their overall experience as satisfied, neutral, or dissatisfied. The results are summarized in the table below.

| Satisfaction Rating | Store A | Store B | Store C | Total |
|---------------------|--------:|--------:|--------:|------:|
| Satisfied | 75 | 65 | 55 | 195 |
| Neutral | 30 | 35 | 40 | 105 |
| Dissatisfied | 15 | 20 | 30 | 65 |
| Total | 120 | 120 | 125 | 365 |

State the null and alternative hypotheses if the store wanted to determine whether the distribution of customer satisfaction ratings is the same across the three store locations.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 🔎 Solution

Just as we have done in past examples, we can take the wording of the problem to help us write the null and alternative hypotheses. In this question, it asks *"determine whether the distribution of customer satisfaction ratings is the same across the three store locations."* Notice the wording of **same** in the question. This is a hint that we will be conducting a test for homogeneity. Remember that the null is that the variable is the same for all populations and the alternative states the variable is not the same for all populations. Using the specific variable and populations for this question, we have:

$H_o:$ The distribution of customer satisfaction ratings is the same across all three stores (Store A, Store B, and Store C)

$H_a:$ The distribution of customer satisfaction ratings is not the same across all three store locations (that is, at least one store has a different distribution of satisfaction ratings).

We can also write the null using probability notation as we did with the goodess-of-fit test.  The hypothesis would be:

$H_o: P_\text{Store A}=P_\text{Store B}=P_\text{Store C}$

where,

- $P_\text{Store A}$ = distribution of customer satisfaction ratings for Store A
- $P_\text{Store B}$ = distribution of customer satisfaction ratings for Store B
- $P_\text{Store C}$ = distribution of customer satisfaction ratings for Store C

$H_a:$ At least one distribution of customer satisfaction is different.

Notice that in either case, writing the hypotheses in words or using probability notation, we do not specify which distribution is different. Therefore, when we conduct the hypothesis test, if the null hypothesis is rejected, we can conclude that at least one store's distribution of customer satisfaction ratings differs from the others. However, the test does not identify which store or stores are different. Additional analyses would be needed to determine where the differences occur.

:::

::: {#exm-exercise-age}
## Exercise by Age Group

Researchers are interested in whether exercise habits differ among age groups. Random samples of young adults, middle-aged adults, and older adults are surveyed and classified according to how often they exercise: never, occasionally, or regularly. The results are summarized in the table below.

| Exercise Frequency | Young Adults | Middle-Aged Adults | Older Adults | Total |
|-------------------|-------------:|-------------------:|-------------:|------:|
| Never | 18 | 25 | 40 | 83 |
| Occasionally | 40 | 45 | 38 | 123 |
| Regularly | 62 | 50 | 42 | 154 |
| Total | 120 | 120 | 120 | 360 |

State the null and alternative hypotheses if the researchers wanted to determine whether the distribution of exercise frequency is the same across the three age groups.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 🔎 Solution

In this question, the researcher wants to *determine whether the distribution of exercise frequency is the same across the three age groups."* We can see that key word **same** indicating that this would be a test for homogeneity.

The hypotheses in words are:

$H_o:$ The distribution of exercise frequency is the same across all three age groups (Young adults, middle-aged adults, older adults)

$H_a:$ The distribution of exercise frequency is not the same across all three age groups (at least one age group has a different distribution of exercise frequency).


The hypotheses using probability notation are: 

$H_o: P_\text{Y}=P_\text{M}=P_\text{O}$

where,

- $P_\text{Y}$​ = distribution of exercise frequency for young adults
- $P_\text{M}$​ = distribution of exercise frequency for middle-aged adults
- $P_\text{O}$= distribution of exercise frequency for older adults

$H_a:$ At least one distribution of exercise frequency is different

:::

### Expected Counts

The calculation of expected counts for a chi-square test for homogeneity is identical to that of a chi-square test for independence. For each cell in the table, the expected count is calculated by multiplying the row total by the column total and dividing by the grand total:

$$E=\frac{(\text{Row Total})(\text{Column Total})}{\text{Grand Total}}$$

As before, expected counts represent the counts we would expect to observe if the null hypothesis were true. In a test for homogeneity, this means we assume that the distribution of the categorical variable is the same across all populations or groups.

### Test Statistic

As with other chi-square tests, the test of homogeneity compares observed counts to expected counts using the same chi-square test statistic:

$$\chi^2=\sum \frac{(O-E)^2}{E}$$

The expected counts are also still calculated using the row totals and column totals of the contingency table, and the degrees of freedom are

$$df=(r−1)(c−1)$$
where $r$ is the number of rows and $c$ is the number of columns.

Although the context differs, the calculations and hypotheses for a test of homogeneity are very similar to those used in a test of independence. The primary difference is that a test of homogeneity uses data collected from multiple populations, whereas a test of independence uses data collected from a single population on two categorical variables.

### P-value Approach

The p-value approach for a chi-square test for homogeneity is identical to the approach used in previous hypothesis tests. After computing the chi-square test statistic and degrees of freedom, obtain the p-value and compare it to the significance level, $\alpha$. 

- If the p-value $\leq \alpha$, reject $H_0$.
- If the p-value $> \alpha$, fail to reject $H_0$.

Rejecting the null hypothesis provides evidence that the distribution of the categorical variable differs among the populations or groups being compared. Failing to reject the null hypothesis indicates that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the distributions differ.

The p-value approach for the chi-square test of homogeneity follows the same hypothesis testing process as the chi-square test of independence. As before, the p-value and test statistic will be found using Rguroo. 

To prepare for the following examples, review the following:

- [General Hypothesis Test Steps](#general-hypothesis-steps)
- [Calculate the p-value and test statistic in Rguroo](#GOF-P-Value_Approach-in-Rguroo)
- [Create a Two-Way Table in Rguroo](#create-tables)

::: {#exm-customer-satisfaction-p-value}
## Customer Satisfaction - P-value Approach

A company operates three retail store locations and wants to compare customer satisfaction among the stores. A random sample of customers is selected from each location and asked to rate their overall experience as satisfied, neutral, or dissatisfied. The results are summarized in the table below.

| Satisfaction Rating | Store A | Store B | Store C | Total |
|:---------------------|--------:|--------:|--------:|------:|
| Satisfied | 75 | 65 | 55 | 195 |
| Neutral | 30 | 35 | 40 | 105 |
| Dissatisfied | 15 | 20 | 30 | 65 |
| Total | 120 | 120 | 125 | 365 |


Help the store determine whether the distribution of customer satisfaction ratings is the same across the three store locations at the $\alpha=0.05$ level of significance. 

:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 🔎 Solution

As we did before with previous $\chi^2$ tests, take a quick check that we have satisfied the four conditions. We will perform the hypothesis test and check in the Rguroo output that all expected counts are greater than 5. Let’s proceed with the test.

**State null and alternative**

$H_o: P_\text{Store A}=P_\text{Store B}=P_\text{Store C}$

where,

- $P_\text{Store A}$ = distribution of customer satisfaction ratings for Store A
- $P_\text{Store B}$ = distribution of customer satisfaction ratings for Store B
- $P_\text{Store C}$ = distribution of customer satisfaction ratings for Store C

$H_a:$ At least one distribution of customer satisfaction is different.

**Select $\alpha$**

$\alpha=0.05$

**P-value approach to find test statistic and p-value**

To conduct the test and check the expected counts, create a two-way table in Rguroo. @fig-satistfaction shows an image of the table in Rguroo.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-satisfaction
#| fig-cap: 'Rguroo Table for Customer Satisfaction by Store'
#| fig-alt: 'Rguroo Table for Customer Satisfaction by Store'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Chi-Square/satisfaction-table.png")
```


Then, select [satisfaction rating]{.var} for [Factor 1]{.fun} and [Store]{.var} for [Factor 2]{.fun}. Leave 0.05 for the significance level.  The dialog box is shown below.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-dialog-satisfaction
#| fig-cap: 'Dialog box for Customer Satisfaction by Store Example'
#| fig-alt: 'Dialog box for Customer Satisfaction by Store Example'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_dialogs/Chi_squared/dialog-homogeneity-satisfaction.png"
)
```



Before looking at the test statistic and p-value, let's check the Rguroo output and verify that the expected counts are all greater than 5.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-expected-counts-satisfaction
#| fig-cap: 'Expected Counts for Customer Satisfaction by Store Example'
#| fig-alt: 'Expected Counts for Customer Satisfaction by Store Example'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_outputs/Chi-Square/expected-counts-homogeneity-satisfaction.png"
)
```

After inspecting the expected counts, we can verify that all expected counts are greater than 5 and the conditions are met. Let's proceed with looking at the output for the p-value and test statistic.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-satisfaction-output-p-value
#| fig-cap: 'Rguroo output for Test of Homogeneity for Customer Satisfaction by Store Example'
#| fig-alt: 'Rguroo output for Test of Homogeneity for Customer Satisfaction by Store Example, showing graph, p-value = 0.04635 and test statistic of 9.67094'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_outputs/Chi-Square/output-homogeneity-satisfaction-p-value.png"
)
```

The P-value graph displays the chi-squared distribution under the null hypothesis. The observed test statistic, $\chi^2 =9.67094$, is marked by the green triangle. The red shaded area to the right of the test statistic represents the p-value, p-value =0.04635.

**Decision**

Since the p-value is $< \alpha$, $0.04635$ is $<0.05$, we reject the null hypothesis.

**Conclusion**

There is sufficient evidence to support the claim that at least one distribution of customer satisfaction is different. This means that there is evidence that the stores do not have the same satisfaction ratings among all three stores.

:::

:::{#exm-sleep-study-homogeneity-p-value}
## Alcohol Use by Gender - P-value Approach

Let's revisit @exm-sleep-study-test-independence-p-value. A sleep study collected information from college students about their sleep habits, academic experiences, and overall well-being. Variables include sleep and wake times, average amount of sleep, class schedules, GPA, classes missed, and measures related to cognition, stress, anxiety, alcohol use, depression, and happiness. Do the data indicate that alcohol use is the same for males and females at the $\alpha=0.02$ level of significance? 

A complete description of the variables is provided in the [dataset code book](#code-book-sleep). 

:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 🔎 Solution

As we did before with previous $\chi^2$ tests, take a quick check that we have satisfied the four conditions. We will perform the hypothesis test and check in the Rguroo output that all expected counts are greater than 5. Let’s proceed with the test.

**State null and alternative**

$H_o: P_\text{Males}=P_\text{Females}$

where,

- $P_\text{Males}$ = distribution of alcohol use for males
- $P_\text{Females}$ = distribution of alcohol use for females

$H_a:$ At least one distribution of alcohol use is different.

**Select $\alpha$**

$\alpha=0.02$

**P-value approach to find test statistic and p-value**

To conduct the test and check the expected counts, use Rguroo's [Contingency Table]{.fun} function. Since this dataset is in the dataset repository, we do not need to create a table.

Select [Gender]{.var} for [Factor 1]{.fun} and [AlcoholUse]{.var} for [Factor 2]{.fun}. Enter [0.02]{.typein} for the significance level.  The dialog box is shown below.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-dialog-alcohol-gender
#| fig-cap: 'Dialog box for Gender and Alcohol Use Example'
#| fig-alt: 'Dialog box for Gender and Alcohol Use Example'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_dialogs/Chi_squared/dialog-homogeneity-gender-alcohol.png"
)
```


Before looking at the test statistic and p-value, let's check the Rguroo output and verify that the expected counts are all greater than 5.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-expected-counts-gender-alcohol
#| fig-cap: 'Expected Counts for Gender and Alcohol Use Example'
#| fig-alt: 'Expected Counts for Gender and Alcohol Use Example'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_outputs/Chi-Square/expected-counts-homogeneity-gender-alcohol.png"
)
```

After inspecting the expected counts, we can verify that all expected counts are greater than 5 and the conditions are met. Let's proceed with looking at the output for the p-value and test statistic.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-gender-alcohol-output-p-value
#| fig-cap: 'Rguroo output for Test of Homogeneity for Gender and Alcohol Use Example'
#| fig-alt: 'Rguroo output for Test of Homogeneity for Gender and Alcohol Use Example, showing graph, p-value = 0.00752 and test statistic of 11.9614'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_outputs/Chi-Square/output-homogeneity-gender-alcohol-p-value.png"
)
```

The P-value graph displays the chi-squared distribution under the null hypothesis. The observed test statistic, $\chi^2 =11.9614$, is marked by the green triangle. The red shaded area to the right of the test statistic represents the p-value, p-value =0.00752.

**Decision**

Since the p-value is $< \alpha$, $0.00752$ is $<0.02$, we reject the null hypothesis.

**Conclusion**

There is sufficient evidence to support the claim that at least one distribution of alcohol use is different. This means that there is evidence that genders do not have the same alcohol use.


:::

### Critical Region Approach

The critical region approach for a chi-square test for homogeneity is identical to the approach used for the chi-square goodness-of-fit test and the chi-square test for independence. Determine the critical value using the significance level, $\alpha$, and the appropriate degrees of freedom, then compare the test statistic to the critical value.
 
- If the test statistic is greater than or equal to the critical value, reject $H_0$.
- If the test statistic is less than the critical value, fail to reject $H_0$.

Just as with the p-value approach, rejecting the null hypothesis provides evidence that the distribution of the categorical variable differs among the populations or groups being compared and failing to reject the null hypothesis indicates that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the distributions differ.

:::{#exm-customer-satisfaction-critical-region}
## Customer Satisfaction - Critical Region Approach

Let's revisit @exm-customer-satisfaction-p-value, but use the critical region approach. A company operates three retail store locations and wants to compare customer satisfaction among the stores. A random sample of customers is selected from each location and asked to rate their overall experience as satisfied, neutral, or dissatisfied. The results are summarized in the table below.

| Satisfaction Rating | Store A | Store B | Store C | Total |
|---------------------|--------:|--------:|--------:|------:|
| Satisfied | 75 | 65 | 55 | 195 |
| Neutral | 30 | 35 | 40 | 105 |
| Dissatisfied | 15 | 20 | 30 | 65 |
| Total | 120 | 120 | 125 | 365 |


Help the store determine whether the distribution of customer satisfaction ratings is the same across the three store locations at the $\alpha=0.05$ level of significance. 

:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 🔎 Solution

Since we are testing the same claim as @exm-customer-satisfaction-p-value, we will use our work from that example and use the critical region output from Rguroo.  In that example, we already checked that the conditions for a chi-squared test were met.

**State null and alternative**

$H_o: P_\text{Store A}=P_\text{Store B}=P_\text{Store C}$

where,

- $P_\text{Store A}$ = distribution of customer satisfaction ratings for Store A
- $P_\text{Store B}$ = distribution of customer satisfaction ratings for Store B
- $P_\text{Store C}$ = distribution of customer satisfaction ratings for Store C

$H_a:$ At least one distribution of customer satisfaction is different.

**Select $\alpha$**

$\alpha=0.05$

**Critical region approach to find test statistic and critical value**

Use the same process as in @exm-customer-satisfaction-p-value, but scroll down to the critical region output in Rguroo.  The output is shown below.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-satisfaction-output-critical-region
#| fig-cap: 'Rguroo critical region output for Test of Homogeneity for Customer Satisfaction by Store Example'
#| fig-alt: 'Rguroo critical region output for Test of Homogeneity for Customer Satisfaction by Store Example, showing graph, critical value = 9.4877 and test statistic of 9.6709'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_outputs/Chi-Square/output-homogeneity-satisfaction-critical-region.png"
)
```

The critical region graph displays the chi-squared distribution. The red shaded region represents the critical region for a $\alpha=0.05$ significance level and begins at the critical value of $\chi^2=9.4877$. The green triangle marks the observed chi-squared test statistic of $\chi^2=9.6709$. 

**Decision**

Because the observed test statistic, $\chi^2 =9.6709$, does fall within the red critical region (values greater than $\chi^2 =9.4877$), the null hypothesis is rejected.

**Conclusion**

There is sufficient evidence to support the claim that at least one distribution of customer satisfaction is different. This means that there is evidence that the stores do not have the same satisfaction ratings among all three stores.

:::

## Code book for Melanoma Dataset

**Description** The Melanoma dataset has data on 205 patients in Denmark with malignant melanoma.

Format

This data frame contains the following columns:

[time]{.var}: Survival time in days, possibly censored.

[status]{.var}: 1 died from melanoma, 2 alive, 3 dead from other causes.

[sex]{.var}: 1 = male, 0 = female.

[age]{.var}: Age in years.

[year]{.var}: Year of operation.

[thickness]{.var}: Tumour thickness in mm.

[ulcer]{.var}: 1 = presence, 0 = absence.

Source
P. K. Andersen, O. Borgan, R. D. Gill and N. Keiding (1993) Statistical Models based on Counting Processes. Springer.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 🔎 Solution

As we did before with previous $\chi^2$ tests, take a quick check that we have satisfied the four conditions. We will perform the hypothesis test and check in the Rguroo output that all expected counts are greater than 5. Let’s proceed with the test.

**State null and alternative**

We will again use the language of the question to help us with the hypotheses. The question is *"Is the distribution of survival status the same for male and female melanoma patients?"* So, we have

$H_o: P_\text{Males}=P_\text{Females}$

where,

- $P_\text{Males}$ = distribution of survival status for males
- $P_\text{Females}$ = distribution of survival status for females

$H_a:$ At least one distribution of survival status is different.

**Select $\alpha$**

$\alpha=0.01$

**Critical region approach to find test statistic and critical value**

This dataset is in the dataset repository; however, [status]{.var} and [sex]{.var} are recorded as numbers.  In order to us these variables in a test for homogeneity, we need to reclassify these as categorical variables and add labels. In this example, we want to label the levels defined in the codebook. [Click here](#reclassifying-variables) to review how to reclassify variables. Teh dialog boxes are shown below.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-dialog-variable-editor-status
#| fig-cap: 'Dialog box for Variable Editor (Status)'
#| fig-alt: 'Dialog box for Variable Editor (Status)'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_dialogs/Chi_squared/dialog-variable-editor-status.png"
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-dialog-variable-editor-sex
#| fig-cap: 'Dialog box for Variable Editor (Sex)'
#| fig-alt: 'Dialog box for Variable Editor (Sex)'

knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_dialogs/Chi_squared/dialog-variable-editor-sex.png"
)
```

Use the [Contingency Table]{.fun} test, and select [Melanoma]{.data} dataset. Select [status]{.var} for [Factor 1]{.fun} and [sex]{.var} for [Factor 2]{.fun}. Enter [0.01]{.typein} for the significance level.  The dialog box is shown below.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-dialog-status-sex
#| fig-cap: 'Dialog box for Status and Sex Example'
#| fig-alt: 'Dialog box for Status and Sex Example'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_dialogs/Chi_squared/dialog-homogeneity-status-sex.png"
)
```


Before looking at the test statistic and p-value, let's check the Rguroo output and verify that the expected counts are all greater than 5.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-expected-counts-status-sex
#| fig-cap: 'Expected Counts for Status and Sex Example'
#| fig-alt: 'Expected Counts for Status and Sex Example'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_outputs/Chi-Square/expected-counts-homogeneity-status-sex.png"
)
```

After inspecting the expected counts, we can verify that all expected counts are greater than 5 and the conditions are met. Let's proceed with looking at the output for the p-value and test statistic.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-status-sex-critical-region
#| fig-cap: 'Rguroo output for Test of Homogeneity for Status and Sex Example'
#| fig-alt: 'Rguroo output for Test of Homogeneity for Status and Sex Example, showing graph, critical value = 9.2103 and test statistic of 6.793'
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics(
  "Rguroo_outputs/Chi-Square/output-homogeneity-status-sex-critical-region.png"
)
```

The critical region graph displays the chi-squared distribution. The red shaded region represents the critical region for a $\alpha=0.05$ significance level and begins at the critical value of $\chi^2=9.2103$. The green triangle marks the observed chi-squared test statistic of $\chi^2=6.793$. 

**Decision**

Because the observed test statistic, $\chi^2 =6.793$, does not fall within the red critical region (values greater than $\chi^2 =9.2013$), the null hypothesis is not rejected.

**Conclusion**

There is not sufficient evidence to support the claim that at least one distribution of survival status is different. This means that the evidence shows that survival status from melanoma is the same among males and females.

:::

## Comparing Chi-Square Tests

Throughout this chapter, we have examined three different chi-square tests: the chi-square goodness-of-fit test, the chi-square test of independence, and the chi-square test of homogeneity. Although these tests address different research questions, they all use the same chi-square test statistic and compare observed counts to expected counts. The primary difference among the tests is the type of question being investigated and the structure of the data. The table below summarizes the purpose of each test and can help you determine which chi-square procedure is appropriate in a given situation.

::: {.callout-note}
## Summary of Chi-Square Tests

| Test | Purpose | Variables | Research Question |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Goodness-of-Fit | Compare data to a claimed distribution | One categorical variable | Does the observed distribution match a specified distribution? |
| Independence | Determine whether two categorical variables are related | Two categorical variables from one population | Are the variables associated? |
| Homogeneity | Compare distributions across populations or groups | One categorical variable measured in multiple populations | Are the distributions the same across groups? |

:::

:::{#exm-determine-type-of-chi-squared-test}
## Determine the Appropriate Chi-squared Test

For each scenario below, determine whether a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, test of independence, or test of homogeneity should be used. Explain your choice.

a\. A researcher wants to know whether blood types in a city follow the nationally reported distribution.

b\. A survey records both a person's employment status and education level to determine whether the variables are related.

c\. A political scientist compares the distribution of party affiliation among voters from three different states.

d\. A restaurant owner compares the observed counts of menu items sold to expected percentages based on historical sales.

e\. A health researcher records smoking status and exercise habits for a random sample of adults and wants to determine whether the variables are associated.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test; The researcher is comparing the observed blood type counts in one population (the city) to an expected distribution (the national blood type percentages). A goodness-of-fit test is used to determine whether the observed distribution matches an expected distribution.

b\. Chi-Square Test of Independence; Two categorical variables are measured from the same sample of individuals: employment status and education level. The goal is to determine whether the variables are *associated*, so a test of independence is appropriate.

c\. Chi-Square Test of Homogeneity; The researcher is comparing the distribution of a categorical variable (party affiliation) across multiple populations (voters from three different states). A test of homogeneity is used to determine whether the distributions are the *same* across the populations.

d\. Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test; The restaurant owner is comparing observed sales counts to an expected distribution based on historical percentages. Since there is one categorical variable and a known expected distribution, a goodness-of-fit test should be used.

e\. Chi-Square Test of Independence; Two categorical variables (smoking status and exercise habits) are measured for the same individuals. The goal is to determine whether there is an *association* between the variables, making a test of independence appropriate.

:::

:::{#exm-chi-square-summary1}
## Patient Satisfaction

Researchers randomly select patients from three different hospitals. Each patient rates their overall satisfaction with their care as dissatisfied, neutral, or satisfied. The researchers conduct a hypothesis test to determine if the distribution of patient satisfaction is the same across the three hospitals at the $\alpha=0.05$ level of significance.

a\. Identify the appropriate chi-square test.

b\. State the null and alternative hypotheses.

c\. If the p-value is found to be $0.12$, state the decision.

d\. Write the conclusion of the test.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. Appropriate Test: Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity

b\. Hypotheses

$H_0: P_1 = P_2 = P_3$

$H_a:$ At least one distribution of patient satisfaction is different.

where:

- $P_1$ = distribution of patient satisfaction ratings at Hospital 1
- $P_2$ = distribution of patient satisfaction ratings at Hospital 2
- $P_3$ = distribution of patient satisfaction ratings at Hospital 3

c\. Decision: Since the p-value (0.12) is not less than $\alpha$ (0.05), we do not reject the null hypothesis.

d\. Conclusion: There is not sufficient evidence to support the claim that at least one distribution of patient satisfaction is different. Therefore, patient satisfaction is the same among all three hospitals.

:::

:::{#exm-chi-square-summary2}
## Movie Popcorn

A movie theater manager believes that customers prefer popcorn sizes in the following proportions:
 
- Small: 25%
- Medium: 40%
- Large: 35%
 
A random sample of customers is observed, and the size purchased by each customer is recorded. The movie theater manager conducts a hypothesis test to determine if the observed customer preferences match the claimed distribution of drink sizes at the $\alpha=0.01$ level of significance.

a\. Identify the appropriate chi-square test.

b\. State the null and alternative hypotheses.

c\. If the critical value is $9.210$ and the test statistic is $\chi^2=11.961$, state the decision.

d\. Write the conclusion of the test.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. Appropriate Test: Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test

b\. Hypotheses

$H_o: P_\text{small}=0.25, P_\text{medium}=0.40, P_\text{large}=0.35$

$H_a:$ he population does not follow the stated distribution

c\. Decision: Since the $\chi^2$ test statistic (11.961) does fall in the rejection region (above the critical value $\chi^2=9.210$), we reject the null hypothesis.

d\. Conclusion: There is sufficient evidence to support the claim that popcorn sizes do not follow the stated distribution of 25% small, 40% medium, and 35% large.
:::

:::{#exm-chi-square-summary3}
## Class Standing and Course Modality

A university surveys a random sample of students and records each student's class standing (freshman, sophomore, junior, or senior) and preferred course delivery method (in-person, hybrid, or online). The university research team conducts a hypothesis test to determine if course delivery preference is associated with class standing at the $\alpha=0.1$ level of significance.

a\. Identify the appropriate chi-square test.

b\. State the null and alternative hypotheses.

c\. If the p-value is found ot be $0.0375$, state the decision.

d\. Write the conclusion of the test.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. Appropriate Test: Chi-Square Test for Independence

b\. Hypotheses

$H_0:$ Course delivery preference and class stading are associated

$H_a:$ Course delivery preference and class stading are independent


c\. Decision: Since the p-value (0.0375) is less than $\alpha$ (0.1), we reject the null hypothesis.

d\. Conclusion: There is sufficient evidence to support the claim that course delivery preference and class stading are independent.


:::
